title: DeepMind's Ithaca raises historians' accuracy at restoring damaged ancient Greek inscriptions from 25 to 72 percent in a test
summary: DeepMind's Ithaca, a deep neural network, raised historians' accuracy at restoring damaged ancient Greek inscriptions from 25 to 72 percent in a test; no source reports an accepted restoration.
account: On 9 March 2022 Nature published Ithaca, a deep neural network built by DeepMind with the Universities of Venice Ca' Foscari, Oxford and Athens. Authors include Assael, Sommerschield, Prag and de Freitas. Ithaca restores missing text in damaged ancient Greek inscriptions and attributes them to place and date. Ithaca restored text with 62 percent accuracy alone and raised historians' accuracy from 25 to 72 percent when they worked with it. It attributed inscriptions geographically with 71 percent accuracy and dated them to within about 30 years. Its average date of 421 BC for a group of disputed Athenian decrees agreed with recent independent re-dating. The cited sources report accuracy studies and a public interface. No cited source reports that epigraphers have accepted a restoration that Ithaca proposed for a specific inscription. In 2024 Eric Cullhed of Uppsala University reran Ithaca in a study posted on arXiv. In the arXiv version he reports that Ithaca reached 60.9 percent top-1 restoration accuracy on a test set shared with the original paper, close to the reported figure. He also reports that Ithaca reached 46.5 percent on six inscriptions edited after its training data were assembled. He reports that a fine-tuned Llama model did slightly better at restoration and worse at place and date. On 23 July 2025 Nature published Aeneas, the successor model from DeepMind for Latin inscriptions. The study by Cullhed appeared in Digital Scholarship in the Humanities on 25 November 2025.

display.answer: The Nature paper and the Ca' Foscari press release come from the developers of Ithaca. Charlotte Roueché, who is not an author, comments on the paper in Nature News & Views. Eric Cullhed reran Ithaca on a test set shared with the original paper. He thanks two Ithaca authors for comments on a draft. The MIT Technology Review report covers Aeneas, the successor model.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: DeepMind's Ithaca, a deep neural network, raised historians' accuracy at restoring damaged ancient Greek inscriptions from 25 to 72 percent in a test; no source reports an accepted restoration.
fields.account: On 9 March 2022 Nature published Ithaca, a deep neural network built by DeepMind with the Universities of Venice Ca' Foscari, Oxford and Athens. Authors include Assael, Sommerschield, Prag and de Freitas. Ithaca restores missing text in damaged ancient Greek inscriptions and attributes them to place and date. Ithaca restored text with 62 percent accuracy alone and raised historians' accuracy from 25 to 72 percent when they worked with it. It attributed inscriptions geographically with 71 percent accuracy and dated them to within about 30 years. Its average date of 421 BC for a group of disputed Athenian decrees agreed with recent independent re-dating. The cited sources report accuracy studies and a public interface. No cited source reports that epigraphers have accepted a restoration that Ithaca proposed for a specific inscription. In 2024 Eric Cullhed of Uppsala University reran Ithaca in a study posted on arXiv. In the arXiv version he reports that Ithaca reached 60.9 percent top-1 restoration accuracy on a test set shared with the original paper, close to the reported figure. He also reports that Ithaca reached 46.5 percent on six inscriptions edited after its training data were assembled. He reports that a fine-tuned Llama model did slightly better at restoration and worse at place and date. On 23 July 2025 Nature published Aeneas, the successor model from DeepMind for Latin inscriptions. The study by Cullhed appeared in Digital Scholarship in the Humanities on 25 November 2025.
